ai_summary: Scotland’s energy generation demonstrates a clear operational contrast against the broader British electricity network today. Total GB wind output stands at 9.7 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 3.8 GW, which represents 37.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust performance pushes Scottish carbon intensity down to an ideal 0 gCO2/kWh, significantly lower than the GB-wide carbon intensity of 108 gCO2/kWh. Despite this abundant zero-carbon generation, transmission bottlenecks prevent clean power from being fully exported to southern demand centers. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 1848.9 MWh, imposing a constraint cost of about £49,372 on the system operator. The resulting deficit forces the grid to rely on thermal generation down south, with an estimated 351291.0 m3 of gas burned elsewhere to replace the restricted renewable volume. This replacement burning counteracts decarbonisation progress by releasing 647.1 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. The situation clearly illustrates the persistent structural friction between renewable capacity in Scotland and national transmission limits, where significant expenditure and avoidable carbon emissions occur simultaneously because clean energy cannot move freely across the boundary to displace thermal generation.
